text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said on Wednesday that an estimated 1998 budget surplus of 10 billion crowns will be used for health care, schools and child and elderly care. He called for municipalities and regional authorities not to lay off teachers, nurses and staff in the elderly care unnecessarily.

- Share funds have decreased their holdings in large companies such as medical and industrial gas group AGA AB and household appliance Electrolux AB while placing new investments in Netcom Systems, Getinge and JM, according to quarterly figures from the newspaper's DN Ownership Service.

- December was, in all likelihood, the last month with disinflation within the forseeable future, according to Lars Jacobsson, head of Swedish Retail and Wholesale Research Institute HUI. In 1997, average annual inflation is expected to be about one percent. The turn comes as positive effects from a cut in Value Added Tax on food to 12 percent from 21 percent as of January 1, 1996. This effect will end in 1997 as this year's prices will be compared to the lower 1996 prices.

- Swedish export companies welcome the stronger U.S. dollar. For the car, forestry and mining sectors -- which have most of their sales in dollars -- the U.S. currency's strengthening by half a crown in three months means a sharp increase in profits. But since many companies have currency hedges, the effect will be delayed.

- Sweden's new Industry and Commerce Minister Leif Pagrotsky promises to sell virtually all of his company shares, worth close to six million crowns, to avoid speculation about him implementing policies for his own benefit.

- Swedish telephone operator Telia AB will not be split up and sold at the moment, according to a government proposal for a new telecommunications law. But the company will have to adhere to tougher rules to stimulate competition.

- Advertising on the Internet will experience its breakthrough this year, according to Peter Bergstrom, foreign markets analyst with the Media Marketing group, Sweden's largest ad broker. A total of 350,000 Swedes surf on the net every day, he said. About two thirds of Sweden's largest advertisers already advertise on the Net, or have plans to do so, according to a survey by Projector New Media KB.

- Saab Aircraft and Hungary agreed on Wednesday to extend their industrial cooperation agreement which expired at the end of 1996. The new agreement will facilitate the possibility of selling Sweden's JAS 39 Gripen fighter to Hungary, according to Saab. Hungary will not decide which fighter it will buy until 1998 at the earliest as it wants to wait to select a plane until after NATO membership negotiations are concluded.

- The Swedish government's policy towards Africa is the subject of a conference called "Partnership Africa" which is being held this week in Abidjan, capital of the Ivory Coast, and will result in a report to the Swedish parliament in the autumn.
